For a step back into the deeply human part of our work, peruse the feature article on the purposes of education. It's an interesting and grounding take on whether we are preparing students for life after school or educating for the intrinsic value of learning (or both).

A few other highlights: science writer Annie Murphy Paul is back with what promises to be a series of compelling research posts on creativity, there's a pairing of posts on professional use of TikTok, find some excellent STEM and humanities pieces and much, much more this week. This is longest Educator's Notebook in the near decade of sharing it.

Enjoy!

2023-03-05.teaser: Humanities in decline? Editing Roald Dahl, retakes
2023-03-05.intro_md:
An extraordinary week.

Much hand-wringing continues about the decline in humanities enrollment in universities, but the feature article from the New Yorker actually paints a less dreary picture in the end than the headline and common discourse suggest. It's a worthy, long read. Also enjoy from the features a short exploration into the perceived cases for and against test corrections and retakes.

In Diversity/Inclusion, find several posts about Black literature and history, and also find several posts about the evolving shape and challenges of DEI discourse today.

Also, in the professional development section, find an extraordinary literature review on how to conduct effective teacher and departmental reviews. One school partnered with the RAND Corporation to deeply study their own review processes -- and then shared the results openly to all. This is an extraordinary gift to other schools and shows both remarkable vulnerability and confidence. My admiration for sharing this work. It will serve and support many schools. The literature review begins on page 15.

These and more, including some very impressive chess mastery in the final post in today's newsletter.

Enjoy!

2023-03-12.teaser: Teachers use ChatGPT more than students, aiEDU launches
2023-03-12.intro_md:
A reflective week.

One of this week's feature posts tells us the story we don't typically hear about the history of science: not the one about the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment, but instead one about global conversation over centuries that led to the innovation in knowledge and technology ultimately centered in some geographies. I'm looking forward to the books it reviews.

The writing on generative A.I. is growing more reflective -- and imaginative. While some may tire of the subject, it's an important one to stay attentive to. The personal computer, mobile device, and internet have changed our classrooms and experiences of learning (for better, for worse), and this will no doubt do the same, but faster and more significantly than the others. Still, while individual technologies may scale and change us more and more quickly, societal change might actually be slowing down. See the tech section(s) for more.

Also, this week is the final issue to include the now-complete series of Exercises for the Recovery of Childhood. I hope this set of poems written by my former colleague Andy Stallings brought you some joy during the pandemic. Visit the [website](https://exercisesfortherecoveryofchildhood.com/) to explore all 62 of them in an interactive space. The Instagram and Facebook pages are far behind and will be updated in the future, so if you want to keep these drops of lightheartedness in your life, consider following them there -- or sharing your email address at the website for a print edition that may come out in the future.

These and many more articles this week,

Enjoy!

2023-03-19.teaser: Question-asking and curiosity, sports injury data
2023-03-19.intro_md:
A remarkable week.

We haven't had this much tech news in the Notebook since we all moved to Zoom -- and that was three years ago this week. This time, two things are happening: first, the education writing space is showing a deeper and deeper understanding of what generative A.I. can do. This means more universities are starting to publish guidelines and resource pages for professors, more independent bloggers are sharing materials on social media, and researchers are digging further and further into generative A.I.'s capacities. And second, ChatGPT-4 was just released this week, and it is an even more powerful tool. See not only the (long) tech section this week, but also the Reading & Writing section, and more.

But also find good pieces this week on topics in general pedagogy -- fostering curiosity, designing good rubrics, and tools for teaching Harkness seminars -- as well as strong pieces on cognitive science, leadership, and more.

Lastly, happy Spring Break to many who may be starting break at this time, and welcome back from Spring Break for the many of you who are just returning, including some visitors who brought students to Jordan over break and stopped by campus. If your school is interested in a trip to the Middle East, don't hesitate to reach out. It's an extraordinary opportunity to develop global perspectives, deepen empathy and understanding, and provide memories for a lifetime.

Enjoy!

2023-04-14.teaser: Your email is not my emergency, generative A.I. now
2023-04-14.intro_md:
A few weeks combined into one...

Enjoy an excellent feature article reminding us that email isn't an emergency and another feature breaking down the experience of using generative A.I. through the eyes of an educator.

I also enjoyed the two articles about the science of math instruction. Pieces on the "science of reading" have been circulating and making waves for several years now. Now mathematics teachers are examining whether a similar approach makes sense in math instruction.

All these and more... enjoy!

Peter

2023-04-21.teaser: Working with your A.I. intern, skipping remedial math
2023-04-21.intro_md:
An excellent week, with fruitful reading for the end of year!

Our feature articles this week focus in the first article on how to begin working with your new A.I. intern/co-pilot, and in the second article on changing philosophy about remedial math work. See the posts for more.

Also, starting this week, I'll begin featuring learning activities: questions, activities, assessments and more. Articles are only helpful in so far as they change practice, and the practice that matters most is what happens between teachers and students. Whether you're inside the classroom or outside the classroom or outside of schools altogether, these might prompt ideas for how to shape what's happening in your own classroom or domain.

Enjoy!

2023-07-03.teaser: Affirmative action falls, the homework apocalypse
2023-07-03.intro_md:
Happy summer and holiday weekend, readers!

It's been an excellent break since the last issue, but I'm returning to the routine. New topics are urgently arising in preparation for this fall, and the news is awash with critical happenings:

• Advances in A.I. continue to complicate learning.

• Advances in A.I. also continue to supercharge learning.

• Supreme Court rulings are challenging diversity efforts.

• Admissions offices are innovating in response.

• The post-pandemic need for good governance grows.

• Social Media continues to cause concern.

• And on the positive and most essential, teaching & learning research continues to yield evidence of what makes for excellent practice.

This week's issue (which catches up on a few previous weeks) captures articles across these topics and much, much more.

On A.I., see the featured blog post by researcher Ethan Mollick on some of the key ways homework will need to evolve in the year ahead. Also see Nate Green's piece in Slate on the need for schools to act now (as in this summer) on how we will proactively set students and teachers up for success in a changed world with A.I.. Green highlights schools' failures (and culture's broader failure) to proactively engage the arrival of social media, and the cost of this is apparent in this week's social media articles, which show the challenges we are still facing today.

Clear policies and practices will help schools engage the emergence of A.I. both responsibly and in ways that empower student learning and teacher growth. Keep an eye on upcoming issues for more on this, and see the featured Learning Activities for the beginnings of a list that I will be accumulating of different practices for students and teachers alike.

Also see the other feature on how admissions offices might pivot in response to the Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action. Affirmative action helped countless students. See also how one student calls for something stronger. The best and boldest find ways to make a better future from even the most difficult losses.

Find all these and much, much more in this week's issue -- including the story of a 14 year old who made his own LEGO animation of Spiderman... and was called on by the producers to animate a scene in the actual film.

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-07-16.teaser: Generative A.I. in mid-2023, Taylor Swift studies
2023-07-16.intro_md:
Happy midsummer, all

It has been two extraordinary weeks -- not just of fireworks and family and friends, but also of developments in A.I. and learning. While the summer is yielding fascinating news and research on teaching and learning, cognitive science, pedagogy and more as always, the A.I. landscape is moving in leaps and bounds. It is almost unbelievable how quickly the field is advancing, and how much both euphoria and doom are circulating in the mediasphere.

For us in education, it is increasingly clear that schools have an enormous opportunity this fall: opportunities for professional growth for teachers, opportunities for customized learning for students, and opportunities for reimagined learning experiences.

It is also clear that every school should be feeling a sense of urgency about preparing for the fall term. This means leadership should be dedicating significant time at opening faculty meetings to share strategies for how the school will proactively navigate the emergence of A.I. Considerations might include:

• Will the school have an organization-wide policy on acceptable use of A.I. -- not only for students but also for faculty and staff?

• What professional learning will ensure all teachers are prepared not only to *respond* to student use of A.I., but to *guide* student use of A.I.?

• Has the school identified a lead team of teachers to drive discussion with the rest of the faculty about use of A.I.?

• What orientation will students have to set clear expectations for use of A.I. across their subjects?

• How will organizations like the school newspaper approach the use of A.I. in student writing? What about the literary magazine?

• Are members of the student life and IT offices prepared to handle student use of AI image and video generation?

I generally avoid grandiose statements about technology, but the world is changing, and it will be important to stay abreast of what is unfolding. If this is your domain, start with the second feature in today's issue, in which Ethan Mollick outlines the state of generative A.I. as of this month. Continue with the articles in the "Tech, AI" section(s) which I will be maintaining for the weeks ahead. Last, I will be slowly incrementally adding activities and exercises to Athena for students and teachers to understand what is possible with the new tools we have access to.

But also: the world remains the same. Human interactions remain the essence of what it means to live our fulfilling lives day to day. The first feature article offers a reminder from Psychology Today on what it means to have intellectual humility, to listen closely to others, and to understand that all people -- even those we vehemently disagree with -- believe their perspective to be true to them. How can we -- especially in a world of artificial intelligence -- remember that emotional intelligence is as much if not more important to living not just fully, but also happily.

So much more to also see this week: the politics of school plays, two pieces on the speed of learning, Taylor Swift studies (?!), pronouncing student names, the return of cursive, the importance of the staff room, and the educational value of board games.

All these and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-07-23.teaser: A teacher's three A.I. uses, Wesleyan ends legacy
2023-07-23.intro_md:
An extraordinary week.

Tech developments in A.I. continue at an explosive pace. Until this rush subsides, I will separate articles on A.I. in schools and relevant developments in other industries into a new section at the end of the newsletter. Some articles about A.I. that are related to other categories will remain in the rest of the newsletter.

Also, I have continued to collect information on A.I. policies and practices -- for schools, teachers, and classes -- on Athena. See the links below for connections to resources on Athena.

In other news, I find an interesting juxtaposition in the social media section: Lawmakers and the Surgeon General are sharing warnings about the significant risks of social media, and students are hosting study sessions on TikTok to stay focused on work. The health risks of social media are real, and yet amid the noise, some students are finding productive practices, too.

See also several interesting pieces on the importance of mid-level leadership. The articles are from industry, but may be equally as resonant to ours.

Finally, in the Other section: find that a large crowd of tourists were stuck in Agatha Christie's home for seven hours. What could go wrong...?

These and others, enjoy!

Peter

2023-07-30.teaser: ChatGPT in schools, affirmative action for the rich
2023-07-30.intro_md:
An excellent week.

Two headlines for this week's issue:

First, see the short essay below for a longer reflection on this moment as it related to A.I. and education. The A.I. world has changed significantly since May, and it's important that schools be prepared.

But also, second, there are major developments outside of tech: legacy admissions is coming under scrutiny, July has been the hottest month in the history of recorded weather, recent research has parsed the efficacy of parent involvement, and more.

In other topics, I'm a particular fan of the podcast by Adam Grant with Ed Catmull from Pixar about creative cultures, and I greatly appreciated the recent Radiolab podcast (and earlier Scientific American article) on the case for how disabilities can become advantages when understood in a different context.

Thanks for reading -- I hope this issue is helpful at this pivotal time. If you find it useful, consider sharing it with colleagues, and if you'd like to subscribe new colleagues to your school, don't hesitate to reach out.

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-08-06.teaser: Is this A.I. moment real? The Classic Learning Test
2023-08-06.intro_md:
A good week as August gets started (including a cartoon about August itself).

The first feature article this week further explores why this A.I. moment may be transformative. This is a helpful read if you or colleagues remain skeptical about this particular hype cycle. The second feature article captures one of the most important themes I've observed in the past several years: the need to focus on discussion and dialogue rather than debate. Written for Middle Web, the piece offers a helpful framework for thinking about the differences between and impacts from debate and discussion.

See also some humor about Roman numerals, an ASCD report on high school schedules, and a brilliant French advertisement for the Women's World Cup.

Last, find a growing collection of featured learning activities for writing with A.I., and a section at the end of the newsletter focused on what else is emerging in the A.I. space.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-08-13.teaser: AI out-creates most of us, structured talk builds agreement
2023-08-13.intro_md:
An excellent week—

Congratulations to those who are already starting up with classes and orientations!

This week’s feature articles focus first on recent research suggesting that with the right scaffolding for conversation, citizens can more easily build bridges across their differences, even when the divide appears large. See the post for what makes this possible, and how we might set these conditions in schools. Also find in the features a post on how we can augment our creativity and innovation with A.I. tools.

Also this week to stay abreast of sustainability efforts, explore the recent collection of articles on renewable energy in the US, including how and why adoption is accelerating — but also why there’s a surprising growing opposition among… environmentalists.

In teaching & learning, see a primer on how academic standards support schools, see examples of what teaching black history looks like in three cities, and more, including featured learning materials, which focus on the African diaspora.

Much more in A.I. this week “below the fold” as the old journalism adage used to go. See especially several posts about turning points in A.I. development.

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-08-20.teaser: The Surgeon General on loneliness, later start times
2023-08-20.intro_md:
Dear Readers,

Since returning to the US, it has been excellent to connect more regularly with colleagues at schools around the country. I’d love to hear more about what your priorities are, and how this newsletter can continue to provide useful resources for you.

Certainly, A.I. is an urgent topic — see a call to action and a forecast for this fall in the section at the end of this issue.

Featured this week is US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy’s report about the epidemic of loneliness. Interestingly, Murthy, who is in his second term as Surgeon General, wrote a book about loneliness before the pandemic, and it was published just after the pandemic began. The whole report is excellent, and there’s a brief section about what education institutions can do.

Also featured is a blog post from the Georgia Tech Admissions office about how university counselors might engage ChatGPT both for their own professional benefit and with students. Writing has been scarce about practical advice for university counseling, and this is a good starting point.

You may have noticed that in this newsletter I generally avoid sensational stories about flare-ups or issues at specific schools — my focus is what is actionable or informative, not what is attention-grabbing — but I’ve included this week the recent NYT piece about a Bay Area school that faced a social media crisis. It’s written in extraordinary detail and offers a meaningful case study both about adolescent experiences with social media and also about how schools can either defuse — or add fuel to — related crises.

See plenty more about SEL curricula, creativity, COVID updates, and an extraordinary ruling in Montana about climate change--because of a lawsuit brought about by students.

Also, a nod to Kim Marshall for his collections on how we teach reading. Find several compelling pieces in the reading/writing section.

Enjoy!

2023-08-27.teaser: NASA's rover challenge, hip-hop at 50, art history
2023-08-27.intro_md:
A full week as summer is winding down.

The feature posts raise an opportunity for STEM students and a fresh look at art history. Worthy to share with the relevant staff in your community.

Also in this issue, find a delightful selection in the humanities, some breathtaking images in STEM that might adorn science classroom walls, and some meaningful data about perceptions of climate change that partners well with a report from NPR on how mandatory climate change education is going in New Jersey.

In tech, find a quiz and outcomes from two surveys on perceptions and understandings of tech in schools and in citizens across the USA.

News about A.I. in schools is naturally spiking, and will continue to do so. See below the fold for a selection from a recent New York Times feature, surveys of students and teachers, and counsel from the blogosphere. The common perception among educators and education leaders is that A.I. will significantly change how learning happens. But the common experience is that they don't feel knowledgeable or prepared. See the section below to get ready.

There's some interesting parallel work happening in, of all places, the copyright industry. I've offered a reflection on this further down below.

All these and others, enjoy!

Peter

2023-09-03.teaser: Caltech accepts Khan Academy, A.I. writes the essay
2023-09-03.intro_md:
Happy Labor Day Weekend in the US!

Extraordinary features this week. The MDRC's research synthesis of what works in High School Reform is an excellent index of what any school leader should be thinking about when fostering excellence at an institution -- and surely most conclusions apply at other levels than secondary.

And the second feature is a first (enormous) signal of the ways in which school requirements, curricula, and student learning may evolve in the years ahead. At Caltech, students can take Khan Academy courses and assessments for some STEM classes for admissions credit without having taken them at their school. It is born of enabling equitable access, which, as is often the case, drives innovation in other settings. There are interesting parallels to students who take AP exams without taking the course. Don't miss the implications of this news, and think about how it might affect your curriculum, diploma requirements, and student learning experience for the years ahead.

See also a helpful triptych of pieces from the NYT on college admissions in the age of Generative A.I. (GenAI).

Also, some fascinating deep dives on relatively obscure topics that offer interesting opportunities for some classes: the geological history of Ukraine, a truly fascinating research project into a pedestrian bridge (how interesting would it be for students to read about the research process itself in a wonderfully detailed narrative like this), and more.

The tech/AI section at the end reflects the growing flurry of writing aimed at guiding schools in their work with GenAI.

And don't miss the several humor pieces this week as lighter fare for a long weekend.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-09-10.teaser: TextFX for writers, Yale rethinks admissions
2023-09-10.intro_md:
An excellent week.

This week's featured articles look first at how to build an institutional research culture at your school. This excellent guide offers useful recommendations from as high level as where Institutional research might fit in an organizational chart to as fine tuned detail as what commands are most useful in Excel. Truly excellent for building and/or developing programs at your school.

The second feature is a new A.I. tool developed by Google in partnership with (brilliant) hip-hop artist Lupe Fiasco to provide a writing assistant for poets, rappers, and other wordsmiths. Enjoy playing with TextFX and deconstructing words, imagining new contexts, juxtaposing imagery, and more.

Elsewhere, find a wealth of provocations that emerged this week: from investigations into the value proposition of college, to challenges to the idea that education enables social mobility, to meta-analyses on the efficacy of trigger warnings, and more.

Also: don't miss in pedagogy the collection of evidence-based approaches to the start of class.

And of course a robust collection of pieces on A.I., both in schools and about developments in the broader industry.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-09-17.intro_md:
Another excellent week.

The features this week include evidence that demand for skills in the marketplace is driving new forms of credentialing in schools. And in the second feature, see an interesting counter example to the personalized learning tide. For the latter, my sense is that no one actually thinks that personalizing our instruction for individual students is bad (it always helps to know individual student progress and to meet them where they are), but as in all things, balance is key. Finding the right balance between collective and individual experiences is a particular joy of course planning.

Also this week, see some provocations about statistics and math teaching in the STEM section, a different take on how we frame DEI work in Diversity/Inclusion, and more.

Last, in the A.I. section at the very end of the newsletter, check out the video of the A.I. service that you upload a video to, and it will translate the video, showing an edited version of you in the video speaking the new language in your voice and changing the movement of your mouth to match the new language. Language teachers take particular note. We live in amazing times.

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-09-24.teaser: Unconditional positive regard, teens advise teens
2023-09-24.intro_md:
An extraordinary week.

Two excellent feature posts: one in which the NYT deep dives on how girls navigate social media today (with a follow up in the section on Adolescence), and another on a helpful frame for what care for kids looks like.

In addition to a host of compelling and provocative pieces this week, see the Workplace section for some interesting commentary on the changes of dress code requirements in the US Senate. I found one opinion piece particularly interesting for its observation that loosening dress codes signifies a drifting away from consensus. This reflects a much larger arc in a shift from the community to the individual. I will be thinking about this for a while. In what ways does/can a dress code show a consensus, a collective agreement about some element of identity that we all share? What might this look like?

Finally, it was a deluge in the tech/AI space this week. The coming weeks will continue to see a surge as students, teachers, and parents begin to reckon with the changing world around us. If you're feeling behind the ball and need to catch up, see the overview by Cornell University. It is comprehensive in context, policy, and practical usage recommendations.

These and others, enjoy!

Peter

2023-10-15.teaser: Teaching the Israel-Hamas war, ACT hits a 1991 low
2023-10-15.intro_md:
Several key notes to kick off this issue:

• A Musical

• Israel and Gaza

• Articles

• A.I.

Musical: Several years ago, I wrote a short musical about schools. For the past two weeks/issues, I was in New York City putting the musical up at the New York Times Center during EdTechWeek. (Thank you for your patience with the absence of newsletters during this time -- long issue this week!). Most of all: what a thrill it was to work with Broadway performers from Hamilton, Moulin Rouge, Six, Aladdin, and a host of other shows for this one-time performance focused on education. I'll share photos and video when they are prepared.

In the meantime, these weeks have been full of education news, and of course global news from the Middle East.

Israel and Gaza: Are you struggling with how to navigate the current situation in Israel and Gaza? See the Features and Humanities section for guidance on how to engage this complex topic with students. In addition to several other resources, also find a link to the Wikipedia article on the Israel-Hamas war. Though it has its shortcomings, Wikipedia continues to one of the most up to date and most factual resources for current events unfolding globally.

Articles: In teaching and learning, find useful pieces on assessment formats, on mobile devices, on group work and more. Also, whether or not you were able to engage the solar eclipse yesterday, don't miss the total eclipse happening this spring. See the STEM section for when it will be and start making your plans.

Of particular interest to me is creator of Calvin & Hobbes Bill Watterson's release of his first book in almost 30 years. In Creativity, find a fascinating video detailing his collaboration with a visual artist to bring it to life. More on the book itself in the Other section.

A.I.: Last, see the A.I. section at the end for another round of extraordinary developments. New technologies continue to emerge at a breakneck pace, and we are entering a new phase of generative A.I. development as schools and industry begin diving more deeply into the practical application of A.I. to their domains.

These and more,

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-10-22.teaser: Should schools make political statements? StoryCorps
2023-10-22.intro_md:
Another full week!

Excellent posts in pedagogy, sustainability, athletics, creativity, leadership, and more.

As the Israeli-Hamas war continues into its third week, schools and colleges are learning from both their initial responses to the crisis and from their efforts to create spaces for students to cope. This week, reflections on these topics surfaced across schools: in leadership, pedagogy, health and more. Echoes are also ringing from the polarization that has marked the recent culture wars in America. See the two feature articles for recent posts about whether schools should make political statements and, perhaps most important in my mind, reflections on how we can reduce polarizations by listening to each others’ stories.

Else in news: a surprising study about the health benefits of cycling in middle school, a pair of posts about cell phone bans, a helpful piece in pedagogy on how personalization can be embedded in whole class work, and another excellent reflection on Barnes & Nobles’ revival that reminds us of the value of decentralization and autonomy in decision making.

Last, see the A.I. section at the end for a case for A.I. not only as pedagogy, but as a topic across the curriculum.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-10-29.teaser: Teachers need a win, the burden of the humanities
2023-10-29.intro_md:
A fascinating week.

The features include a meaningful reflection on the humanities and a crisp reminder to celebrate teachers.

In this week's articles, find new data about the SAT, ideas for the upcoming Mexican holiday Dia de los Muertos, a raft of useful humanities links, practical pedagogical tips, and several posts about adolescent mental health, both in the Adolescence section and in Social Media. The theme of mental health also extends into the Gallup survey near the end suggesting that almost a quarter of the world feels lonely today.

These posts and more, including growing movement in A.I. governance in the A.I. Update at the end,

Enjoy!

Peter

2023-11-12.intro_md:
An excellent week.

I'm (selfishly) featuring this week a blog post I wrote in which I read Disney's "The Sorcerer's Apprentice" through the lens of our current cultural moment with artificial intelligence. The tale, in which Mickey plays a hapless apprentice wielding powerful magic, is actually nearly 2000 years old and has been adapted and readapted over the centuries. A cautionary tale, it prompts meaningful questions for us to ask today. It's the second feature below. I hope you'll check it out.

Also featured this week is some provocative work coming out of Teachers College about the effect of student choice and character complexity on reading. See the first feature below.

Also this week: reflections on assessments, re-conceiving the humanities, cognitive science reminders, and more.

And, some big moves in the A.I. update at the end, including individually customizable bots coming from OpenAI, a White House Executive Order, new prompt frameworks, and more.

All these, enjoy!

Peter

2023-11-20.teaser: Build your own rankings, 180 A.I. class warmups
2023-11-20.intro_md:
Happy Thanksgiving week to American readers!

Our feature articles this week start with a tool for custom college lists that you can create with an interactive database smartly made by The New York Times. Also find a tactical take on how to have productive disagreements on sensitive topics, as guided by two leaders from the NYU School of Law.

Elsewhere in this issue, find three interesting pieces on apprenticeships and work-based learning in the Curriculum and Other sections. Also, November is Native American Heritage Month — find an excellent resource in Diversity/Inclusion with approaches to integrating resources from Native American history in your classes. Last, see two compelling pieces in the STEM section on math pedagogy: one on how we conceive of math instruction at a high level, and another on effective components of math games.

In this week’s A.I. Update, check out how the arrival of A.I. is renewing the importance of the Humanities. Also, find a few helpful takes on the Sam Altman/OpenAI whirlwind weekend.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-11-27.teaser: Drafting an A.I. policy, cursive comes back
2023-11-27.intro_md:
Welcome back from break, readers.

A quieter week this week, but with some gems nonetheless. In the spirit of Thanksgiving, this week's lead article offers advice for ways to show gratitude in your school or organization. This week's second lead article picks up from the A.I. section a post on how motivation will likely play a role in student success with A.I. -- as it has with many previous technological developments.

I'd also like to highlight a workshop that I'll be helping lead with Athena and the African Diaspora Consortium. If you are interested in incorporating materials about the African Diaspora into classes at your school, and especially (but not limited to) AP Capstone Seminar courses, check out the workshop on December 13, linked below in the diversity/inclusion section. Learn more [here](https://eventreg.collegeboard.org/event/fa851fda-0aa8-4793-a02c-df9083897474/summary?SFMC_cid=EM1074695-&rid=43238920) .

Also this week, find a helpful reminder on the role of prior knowledge in learning. See also a thoughtful piece on the importance of teamwork in teacher success.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2023-12-03.teaser: Course-level GPTs, a history of the lecture
2023-12-03.intro_md:
Happy December, Readers.

Two excellent features this week: one looking forwards, one looking backwards. In the first, see how some schools are reimagining how teachers work in order to spark collaboration and motivation. In the second, see a brief reflection by historian of education Larry Cuban on the durability of lectures and questions as core means of learning.

Also this week, find several articles about the outcomes of education. In Curriculum, one post focuses on employment and the other focuses on civics. In Humanities, two pieces take different stances on the purpose of the humanities. And in the AI section, find a piece on the potential impacts of AI on democracy.

Also, here is another reminder: if you are interested in learning more about how content about the African Diaspora might fit in your courses, check out the workshop on December [13](https://eventreg.collegeboard.org/event/fa851fda-0aa8-4793-a02c-df9083897474/summary?SFMC_cid=EM1074695-&rid=43238920) hosted by the African Diaspora Consortium (ADC) and the College Board. This is especially useful if you have AP Seminar courses at your school. I'll be helping run this session on behalf of Athena, where the ADC/College Board partnership keeps its teaching content.

2024-03-03.ai_intro_md:
Artificial intelligence is moving faster, getting bigger, and devouring more, but humans learn at only one speed — ours. Every teacher knows this difference, but technologists, sometimes imagining a Matrix-like world in which we can upload information, often forget.

While we can summon any piece of information from the internet, until we slowly and deeply engage with it, we will not have mastered it enough to transfer what we learn to other settings. Recent research seems to be bearing this out: no one is a “fast learner”, we just have different starting points. Indeed, learning science reminds us that spacing and interleaving over time is necessary for longer term retention: Students forget what they cram; they remember what they recursively return to. Technology is fast, but learning is slow. It takes time.

Similarly, anyone who has led an initiative at their school knows it takes time for adults, too, to understand a new idea, to take individual ownership of it, to integrate it into their work and lives, and to share that understanding with others. Meaning making is a deliberative process. The social and emotional experience of collective learning and professional development is slow.  It takes time.

What does this mean?

Now, in a time of emerging artificial intelligence, narratives are emerging about accelerating learning and about revolutionizing the experience of school, and these narratives should be challenged. The brain works the same way it has for thousands of years. AI tools can interact with it in different ways, but the building of knowledge, skills, habits, and character will remain a slow, iterative, and social process.

AI does invite opportunities for removing administrative distractions for students and teachers alike, and it is full of promise to support and enhance the learning experience. Further still, it may provide more personalized opportunities for students to engage materials on their time and at their own inspiration. This creates more opportunities for learning and more pathways for learning, but it does not accelerate the process of learning — at least not the kind of learning that matters most.

In this spirit of following both the speed of the industry and the speed of humans, schools I have been speaking with have been moving quickly to set clear but flexible guardrails while allowing more space for teachers to engage and experiment deliberately. Now is the time to look to the end of the year, the summer, and the start of next year as growth opportunities to align the practice of AI with its now more clearly apparent promise.

This in mind, enjoy the slower pace of this quiet week: just three posts in this AI section.

The feature articles below contrast each other: the first article describes the blowback from Google’s image generator, and the second article reports on research indicating that people find AI content as reliable as human content.

#### More powerful models, AI optimism and pessimism, On not using AI detectors, and more

This is the year when different sectors work out ways in which AI really can and cannot provide value. AI has been around long enough, and people have had time in different setting to experiment, that value starts to surface. And what I love most of all, is that in this time we begin to see more surprising and specific use cases.

One remarkable piece of data that emerged recently is in the post below in Uses and Applications about how AI can durably reduce conspiracy theory thinking. One study found that people inclined to conspiracy theories had their beliefs lastingly changed by having conversations with AI about their theories. The research showed that AI effectively acknowledges the thinking of the individual, neutrally provides contrary fact, and talks through the ideas with individuals.

What is it about AI that makes it more effective than people at reducing conspiracy thinking in people? Perhaps when we are confronted by others about our beliefs, we feel a need to defend them rather than consider them logically? Perhaps it has to do with the way many AI tools are designed to mirror their conversation partner before introducing something new?

Either way, what strikes me is the growing number of use cases for AI to intermediate with humans for their well being, such as the post in this issue about AI and counseling, which has also appeared in previous issues. While there remains great risk in AI being used conversationally for harm, it is notable that positive use cases are also emerging.

These and much, much more in this issue, enjoy!

#### State of the industry reports, New models, and Global perspectives on AI

The technology continues racing ahead, and policies are slowly catching up.

Stunning developments have emerged in recent weeks, including Udio’s new music generation tool and Microsoft just-unveiled research on lifelike deepfake technology. Learn more about both of them below.

Also this week, Meta released its newest model, Llama3, on all of its platforms, so now every user of Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp has an AI chatbot built into their smartphone apps. What this will do for accessibility to AI is unprecedented.

It’s worth reflecting on the impact of Meta’s decision for the global AI landscape. More than 3 billion people are reported to use Meta’s app universe daily. Only a fraction of them are in developed nations. Significantly, public opinion about generative AI ranges widely across countries; while developed nations are more suspicious of generative AI, emerging nations are more excited about it. This may be natural given what a leveling force generative AI has already proven to be — emerging nations see this as an opportunity to have access to what developed nations take for granted. Now, Meta’s decision to make a powerful LLM freely accessible to all its users massively expands access to AI. What will the outcome be? We’ll see. In the meantime, happy Q&A with Llama3 in Facebook, Messenger, Instagram and WhatsApp!

Also of particular interest this week is Stanford Human-Centered AI Lab’s report on the State of AI. Check out the lab’s findings across a host of topics, including ways in which scientific research has accelerated with the use of AI.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

Excellent updates, including a harrowing story of how an employee created a deepfake recording of a principal in a social revenge event (the first feature), and an emerging understanding of intellectual property may be applied to works created with AI (the second feature). But I want to take a step back for just a moment. In his reflection on the recent ASU GSV conference, EdTech Insider’s Ben Kornell [wrote that](https://edtechinsiders.substack.com/p/the-edtech-insiders-rundown-of-asugsv) “the Cambrian Explosion of AI in edtech is entering a Darwinian moment.” This is a perfect characterization. Last year, AI technology exploded with vision and opportunity, and with remarkable speed, edtech companies burst out of the woodwork. This year, teachers and schools will be assessing these new edtech tools to assess which will survive. In the next two years, the field will narrow and other forms will emerge. But what’s most compelling to me is that schools have the opportunity to determine what survive. This is the time when teachers and leaders provide feedback to the industry to direct it to what actually helps.

But perhaps as a friend of mine said, if we’re coming out of the Cambrian explosion and into Darwinian natural selection, then is the next stage the AI domination? Well, we’ll see.

2024-05-26.ai_heading: On the Simultaneous Embrace For and Pushback Against AI
2024-05-26.ai_intro_md:
As we near the end of the first full year with AI, and while the AI sector continues to catapult forward, the teaching profession is coming to what I see as a double sided approach to the technology: both a warm embrace and a stark red line.

The warm embrace comes from educators who have truly spent time with the technology, who have come to understand its opportunities and limits, and who have recognized how it has the capability to support the work that we do. What may seem controversial now is that this will eventually be all educators. The embrace will look different for each person, but AI will pervade so much of our workflow, and it will support us in ways that will seem second nature in the future: perhaps in our research work, perhaps in our planning, perhaps in our administrative tasks, but inevitably in numerous ways for each person. This is the warm embrace.

At the same time, the stark red line is also becoming more clear. While technophiles pronounce the obsolescence of teachers, it is patently clear to those of us who work with students — and it is increasingly important to state definitively — that students will always need teachers. Real, human teachers. The featured post by John Spencer in the main section of this newsletter makes this case clearly. The piece by New York Times film critic Alissa Wilkinson featured here below also makes a similar statement. AI will continue to provide new and more ways to support teachers, but the relational component of teaching and learning will always require human connection.

In this light, this week’s two features offer compelling provocations. The first piece — “Ninety Five Theses On AI” — offers an excellent set of talking points and topics for individual or class research. Each statement is worth a full discussion. Much of it is technical, but all of it prompts questions about the what the future might look like and what the best paths forward might be. And the second feature asks what it means for technology to look and feel and sound increasingly human. Written by a film critic, the piece reflects on the new ChatGPT and its remarkable semblance to the movie “Her.”

These and more — including some leaps forward by OpenAI and Microsoft, as well as the announcement that Khan Academy’s teacher tools are now fully free — enjoy!

Peter

#### AI Counselors, New Models, and More

Another remarkable week.

Products keep evolving, new models keep coming out, new tools keep emerging. All are true this week.

I think most notable, however, is that we’re seeing more and more of the emergence of AI as a counseling resource. Now, stories and data are becoming more concrete and reaching more readers. The recent TED AI podcast about Woebot is one excellent example. Further, for some remarkable history on this topic, see the final linked article on ELIZA, the first AI chatbot therapist from the 1960s(!).

Also, Eric Hudson’s writing continues to offer strong direction for schools. His four priorities for human-centered AI distill key principles for schools to be thinking about today. Don’t miss these if you are planning your school’s AI strategy.

Lastly, I’m so glad to read from creator of Everything is a Remix Kirby Ferguson his note on the copyright cases by the music industry. It will take time for the various industries to figure out this moment, but I believe Kirby is correct that the ingestion of other creative works is simply a part of the creative process. Certainly, the scope of what can be consumed by machines is greatly increased, but its process mirrors what we do as people; we are inevitably — *always* — influenced by commercial, proprietary works that we encounter and are not licensed to use. But this only informs our creative work and it is not a violation of copyright to witness, be inspired by, and even emulate (to a degree) other copyrighted artwork. It would be a mistake to think anything otherwise. That said, while it would be unwise to criticize newly created works by artists or machines influenced by commercial music or art, there may yet be successful cases brought against companies who train on proprietary content without permission — but that is separate from the mistaken notion that a work created by AI is itself somehow corrupted.

So: the AI sector continues to grow and evolve. It will be a remarkable summer, I’m sure, and by the start of school in the fall, we will inevitably be facing further questions still.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

#### Synthetic relationships, using AI as a crutch, and more

Two major themes this week:

First is the growing awareness of student use of AI for synthetic relationships. Character-based, generative AI technologies are increasingly a part of student lives: as friends, therapists, intimate partners, and more. This is a trend to be aware of — and I was about to say it is also a trend “to get ahead of,” but I’m not certain that anyone yet fully knows what it means to get ahead of this emerging behavior. Both harmful and helpful use cases are emerging, and it will take some time to work out what the role of character-driven generative AI technology is and ought to be in our students’ — and our — lives.

Also this week, find the beginnings of research on the efficacy of generative AI for both student learning and teacher preparation. For learning, the feature article shows how use of GenAI tools can harm students when they use it as a replacement for learning, and it can help them when they use it to augment learning. This seems to be similarly reflected in teacher productivity with generative AI. Teachers who use generative as a partner in designing lessons and preparing for class seem to have their productivity boosted. Those who use generative AI purely for delegating appear to have their productivity worsened. See the studies and articles this week for more.

Also this week, deepfakes and AI based deceptions are hitting the mainstream. Try your hand at two quizzes to see if you can spot AI generated writing and images.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

The first feature this week offers a fascinating look at the effect of conversation with chatbots on conspiracy theories. I shared research on this earlier in the year, but this post dives a little further and shares potential future strategies for leveraging this effect at larger scale.

Also in the features is some early research on the impact of genAI on learning. The report indicates, perhaps as expected, that students with generic AI tools complete work much faster, but then perform worse on assessments without AI, clearly showing that they used AI to circumvent learning. But less reported is that the students who used a generative AI tool that was prepared to act as a tutor (not giving answers directly, for example) performed equally well on assessments later on, but also were significantly more productive when using the tool. This might be an early indicator that generative AI that is properly prepared for learning can aid with student productivity without inhibiting learning, even if it doesn’t enhance learning.

2024-09-29.intro_md:
#### Inspiration, polarization, habit stacking in schools, and more

An excellent week.

I remember a faculty meeting after the Charlottesville “Unite the Right” rally in which discussion centered on the growing polarization we saw in students and society. How might we navigate this polarization as a school, we asked. During the meeting, someone recalled the essay in the Washington Post “The white flight of Derek Black,” in which a white nationalist student at a Florida university, through invitations to and participation in a series of Shabbat dinners, came to build meaningful relationships across difference and eventually renounce his white nationalism. It was the building of relationships through stories that changed him.

Stories and shared experiences, time and again, have seemed the essence of how to build bridges across difference. When I worked briefly in politics, in the time leading up to an election, we were guided not to argue for our candidate when talking to undecided voters, but simply to tell the story of when we decided we would support that candidate.  That would be enough.  And now, in this week’s features, find more about the recent work of StoryCorps and how the organization behind the archive of 350,000 conversations is building conversational experiences intentionally designed to break down the barriers we have built in our culture.  How can we build more opportunities in our schools for students to share experiences together and tell their stories?

Also in the features this week, enjoy a light and lively video about how the principles of game design might be leveraged to shape learning experiences.

Elsewhere in this issue: A baseball fan explores the nature and value of inspiration, a “new” composition by teenage Mozart is found in a library (230+ years later!), a teacher makes the case for how educators might intentionally build “habit stacking” into classes, the social media landscape for adolescents continues to undergo corrections and convulsions, and much more.

Plus, in the AI update, find further astonishing developments and a helpful dive into Bloom’s Taxonomy in the AI era.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
2024-09-29.ai_intro_md:
#### Innovation catapults onward, pedagogy continues to evolve

The story of wonder this week seems to be NotebookLM’s ability to create a full podcast from a source document. What does that mean? Upload source material, and the model will create a dialog-driven podcast in which hosts talk to each other about the topic you’ve designated. Find this and many more surprising use cases at Google Labs, and read more about it in Marc Watkins’ post in this week’s features.

Also in the features, find the education warhorse Bloom’s Taxonomy with a helpful breakdown of how it might be intentionally engaged in an age of AI. Elsewhere in this issue, find how some people are using deepfakes for constructive purposes (in Education), while others are using it for harmful purposes (in Ethics and Risk).

Last, while reading one essay about how researchers are trying to reduce hallucinations by tethering AI to the natural world, I recalled Emerson’s essay “Language.”  In it, he reflects on the idea that words are signs of natural fact, that even when describing abstract ideas, words draw their meaning from their representation of relationships in the natural world. Today, new generative AI technology extends this kind of thinking.  Generative AI tools draw their power from the “models” that map relationships between words.  How might Emerson’s ideas help ground discussions today about the ways AI represents reality?

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

I had seen examples of organizations exploring AI simulations of students for the purpose of allowing teachers to practice lessons live, but I hadn’t yet seen posts exploring the idea that an instructional designer could take a lesson idea and ask a generative AI to imagine classrooms of different sizes and composition experiencing that lesson, thereby creating something like a weather forecast for your lesson plan.

Also this week, see Maha Bali’s exploration of cultural hallucination bias. It is widely understood by now that the nature of AI’s training set leads to inherent biases within AI models, but many people may not yet understand the lived experience of this. Maha explores a few direct experiences of what this means.

2024-10-21.ai_intro_md:
#### How we talk about tech, what risks are growing, how AI is powered, and more

So much of our discourse around AI reflects a binary “with us or against us” mindset. Many people are “for” AI, and many others are “against” it. This is a mistake, of course, as is binary thinking in most complex conversations. In this week’s AI section, find several posts that aim to help us move away from this kind of binary thinking.

In the features, Maha Bali’s chapter on cake-making as an analogy for how we use AI in the classroom brilliantly offers a spectrum of approaches, from “making from scratch” to buying a cake complete from the bakery. When might we bake from scratch, and why? When might we pick up a cake from the store and why? And the natural analogy: when might learn completely by hand? And when might we learn aided by artificial intelligence? Bali dives more deeply into the kinds of questions the analogy poses for how we practice our learning in schools.

Also in the features, find an edge case that highlights risks of vague AI practices and policies. The conditions for this court case are extreme, but worth considering how outcomes are experienced on a smaller scale in most school cases.

Also this week, find Miriam Reynoldson’s helpful practice of “affirmative critique” as an aid to talking with colleagues about AI, find harrowing evidence of the risks of AI, find a detailed description by Sequoia Capital of agentic reasoning, which promises to be the next phase of AI development, and much more, including one doctor’s reflection on how generative AI does better at the human work of bedside conversations with patients than he does.

#### Professional development, media literacy, the election -- and go vote!

A full and rich issue!

This week’s features are short but good ones — one is a brief post on professional development by the teaching & learning blog at the Chronicle of Higher Ed. It summarizes simply what drives ongoing improvement in teaching & learning. When we think about supporting teachers, it really comes down to these few pieces. The second feature then reflects how students today are navigating the glut of information (true and false) in today’s mediascape. It’s important to note in this post that the kids are calling loudly for help in media literacy. They want to talk about and learn how to navigate the world they are in. Interestingly, Nicholas Carr addresses an element of this in the post in Learning Science on two different types of information overload.

The Election. It’s a big week. Find four helpful posts, from an overview of how the electoral college works to a video essay about why voter fraud doesn’t happen at large scale. Also included is a refresher document on how to prepare for a contentious election.

But if there’s one thing I’d like to raise to your attention, it’s one of the features in the AI section at the end. I’ve been working with school boards and leadership teams over the past several months on a presentation and discussion on macro-environmental forces shaping schools today and likely to shape schools in the coming 10-20 years. The topic that I spend the most time on is not AI and the classroom, but the advent of AI companions. I wrote two posts in [August](https://educatorsnotebook.com/issues/2024-08-25#ai-update) and [September](https://educatorsnotebook.com/issues/2024-09-08/#ai-update) about the early signals of the extraordinary impact AI companions are already having on people, and in the past two weeks, the worst case scenario arrived, faster than I expected. Read the features in the AI Update about a teen who commit suicide after growing obsessed with an AI companion. More of your students are meeting social needs with AI than you likely expect. Schools need to be especially attuned to both the positive and negative implications of synthetic relationships.

Really, there’s so much in this issue, from strategic planning tips to cultivating a “just try it” classroom to career and technical curriculum and more.

#### Politics, debate, and discussion in the classroom; Character, college, and more

Helpful posts this week —

After a complicated week on school campuses, find a number of posts about managing complex issues and emotions in school communities. More specifically, I’ve been writing for a number of years about the difference between debate (which has a winner and a loser) and discussion (which aims to arrive and shared understanding, if not necessarily agreement). This week’s issue includes a number of articles that span across and stretch beyond this spectrum:

* See Dan Meyer’s feature article on the unavoidably political nature of the classroom. We are practicing politics in our classroom every day in the way we design our learning experiences and engage student voice. See the feature for more.
* Also in the features, see a documentary by PBS on the growth of debate as a pedagogy for building both reasoning skills and civility across difference. Debate surely has an important place in helping students build and shape evidence-based arguments.
* At the same time, see the article in Pedagogy on discussion across difference. How do the strategies in this post further acknowledge the different lived experiences we have, while also providing guidance for how to advance discussion-based discourse during these complicated moments?
Also this week, I was surprised to see an article suggesting that the price of college is going down. While there appears to be a decline of tuition costs in public universities, the article acknowledges that these are because of increased subsidies that counteract rising costs. How reliable these subsidies will be in the future is unknown, and the underlying economics of the rising cost of education appear to be unchanged. This remains an essential topic for every school leader.

For the classroom, find increasingly helpful and nuanced resources on teaching and learning with AI in the AI Update.

Last, someone actually took the time to calculate whether a room full of monkeys would ever actually be able to write a Shakespearean play. I’m grateful the world has enough people in it that someone had the time and desire to look at this question as scientifically as they did, and then publish their findings. A welcome, light bit of science and math that also honors the humanities.

These and more, enjoy.

Peter
2024-11-10.ai_intro_md:
#### AI in instructional design

Last year, I circulated posts suggesting that we were going through a Cambrian explosion of AI technologies and that this year would be the Darwinian natural selection of AI technologies. In other words, this year and the years ahead would be a time of identifying when and how generative AI tools would actually provide value. It appears to be playing out this way. This week’s AI Update is full of increasingly focused use cases and evaluation of use cases.

In the feature section, find Dr. Philippa Hartman’s methodical assessment of how GenAI tools help with planning, and also see an excellent approach to including AI within assignments. Then find additional helpful use cases in the Tech/AI: Education section.

Elsewhere, an article near the end shares how Google recently revealed that a quarter of all code created by Google engineers is generated with AI. Since it is full of early tech adopters, the coding environment is a good advance view of what a future of generative AI supported writing might look like.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2024-11-25.ai_intro_md:

2024-12-01.teaser: Australia sets social media age at 16, disagreeing well
2024-12-01.intro_md:
#### Minimum social media age, productive disagreement, classroom collaboration and more

Short week, big news!

In an enormous move, Australia last week formalized a minimum age of 16 for social media use. Starting in late 2025, social media companies will be required by lawmakers to verify the age of their users or receive fines. Read more in the features. Also in the features, explore the post about productive disagreement, including ways to engage in discussion on polarizing topics.

Also this week, find stories of grit and resilience, ways to think about delegating, approaches to fostering intrinsic motivation, and more.

In the AI Update, find one of the best overviews of the opportunities and risks of generative AI in schools, as well as further detailed visions of how GenAI can fit within daily pedagogy.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
2024-12-01.ai_intro_md:
#### Teaching & learning with AI gets more focused, creating an AI replica of yourself, and more

In this week’s features, find the best summary I’ve seen yet about the positive and negative narratives surrounding AI, including high level tips for application of these narratives and critical insight into each one. Also in the features, see a wonderfully detailed dive into appropriate use of generative AI for developing literacy in elementary schools. Note that the recommendations are clear that students in elementary school should not use generative AI themselves, but that generative AI can be a strong support for teachers at these grade levels. See the report for more detail, including examples and instructions.

Also this week, find more and more remarkable uses and applications of generative AI, including the development of replicas of our own personalities. Researchers at Google’s DeepMind suggest that after a two-hour interview with a chatbot, the chatbot can respond to personality questionnaires and tests with 85% accuracy. Looking to question yourself on a particular topic? Maybe one day you’ll be able to approximate it. What a wild, weird world we are entering — we may soon be able to have ourselves as our own assistants.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2025-01-06.intro_md:
#### Happy New Year!

Happy 2025, Readers!

To me, anything beyond the year 2000 still feels like the distant future, and yet, here we are 25 years later. Tempus fugit!

I’m excited to share a number of announcements in the weeks and months ahead, but will start the year off with just a brief introduction to this issue. More soon.

In the meantime, enjoy this issue to start of the year!

Peter

This week: The two feature articles both focus on pedagogy, as a reminder that teaching and learning are ultimately what school is about. In one post, find a reminder that balancing high expectations and support for students is at the very center of good teaching. And in the other post, find a reminder that providing autonomy within the context of high expectations and support helps students develop agency. (To this day, Daniel Pink’s book “Drive,” about intrinsic motivation, is the book that has most influenced my teaching.)

Elsewhere in this issue, find several year-in-review posts, find posts on diversity efforts in our new climate, and find a remarkable report on the rebirth of Notre-Dame, including a history of its construction.

Also this week is an article on pornography and adolescence. This is a complicated topic, and sometimes even mentioning it turns people away, but it’s important for adults in schools to know how pervasive pornography is in adolescent lives today — and the advent of generative AI makes it even more complicated. See the Adolescence section for more.

Last, at the end of this issue are some stunning developments in AI, as people begin turning to AI for spirituality, as people’s engagement with AI as social companions deepens, and as uses cases for AI in instructional design begin cohering.

All these and more, enjoy!

Peter
2025-01-06.ai_intro_md:
#### New Year, New Developments

While much is made today about the effect of AI on teaching and learning — and while it will take time for our profession to adapt to this technology (it took more than 20 years for math teaching to adjust to the arrival of the calculator) — the greatest impact of AI will be on our social world, for students and adults alike. This week’s features show continued glimmers of our AI-filled future.

One feature post shows early signs of the role AI will play in people’s spiritual lives. Anything that is not easily explained has a touch of the mystical — it’s how humans ascribed meaning to the moon and stars for centuries — and it seems inevitable that people will put their faith (literally) in AI. See how this is already beginning.

Also in the features, read extraordinary reporting from the Verge on how AI companions are playing surprising roles in people’s lives — with all the benefits and risks that come with it.

And with teaching & learning, find a number of useful resources, especially Dr. Philippa Hardman’s informal survey of what works for instructional design.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2025-01-15.teaser: TikTok harm 'at industrial scale,' AI's 2024 in review
2025-01-15.intro_md:
#### Teaching & learning, LA wildfires, executive orders, and more

A short but packed issue this week.

Over the past several months, I have been in conversation with dozens of school leaders about their upcoming teaching & learning priorities. At the head of most lists are 1) managing artificial intelligence in teaching and learning and 2) supporting civil discourse. I’ll write more about the former in the weeks ahead, but will highlight the latter here.

Most schools are expecting that next week’s inauguration will be followed by a series of **executive orders** that will prompt questions and strong reactions from students and faculty alike — and are exploring either how these moments might become learning experiences or how they might be acknowledged and moved on from.

**If you’re looking for approaches to acknowledge current events and move on** from them, you might visit a growing body of resources for teachers we are aggregating at the [**Current Events topic on Athena Lab**](https://app.athenalab.io/topics/67). This includes approaches from dozens of teachers ranging from simple acknowledgement to more involved collaborative engagement with the news.

**If you’re looking to explore more deeply the historical context and significance** of executive orders (from the Emancipation Proclamation to the Japanese Concentration Camps during World War II), you might find useful the short list of resources we have gathered at the [**US Presidential Executive Orders topic on Athena Lab**](https://app.athenalab.io/topics/1308). This topic is new, and we would welcome recommendations for other resources or approaches you may be taking, too.

Further, teachers of humanities subjects and teaching & learning leaders at their schools have started forming groups on Athena Lab in order to build **networks of teachers across schools** to reduce isolation and support growth and collaboration. If you are interested in learning more about this growing group, just reply to me, and I will send further information.

~

To this week’s articles:

Find a feature on how to effectively use work periods in class and another on the growing understanding of the harm of certain social media behavior.

Also this week: a rich section on character, on humanities, on reading and writing, and more, including several visual explorations of the LA wildfires. See also two different approaches to classroom observations. I find particularly interesting the reading list from Stanford on productive disagreement (in Curriculum) and the provocative piece against institutional neutrality (in Humanities).

These and much more, enjoy!

Peter
2025-01-15.ai_intro_md:
#### Short update, useful resources

In this week’s short AI Update, find two excellent features: First, for an overview of the big stories in AI from 2024, peruse Claire Zau’s lengthy (but segmented) round up of stories from across the AI/Education sector: from technological developments to moments that spread across the public consciousness and more.

For a more practical view, explore the AI Edu Pathways post for first hand reports on how professors have used AI transcripts as objects for evidence of learning. What questions do students ask to generate strong outcomes? How do they critically assess and follow up on the work produced by AI? And crucially: how do the instructors manage the process of assigning and reviewing this kind of work?

Elsewhere, find a few posts on emerging legal questions, new use cases for AI, and one instructional designer’s experience using generative AI as practice students, so she can try out some of her work on simulated students before engaging with actual students in class.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2025-01-19.intro_md:
#### MLK Day, the inauguration, virtual tutors, virtual companions, creative writing, and more

A short but packed issue.

In this week’s features, explore Dan Meyer’s excellent demonstration of how to make math lessons personal. Note, this doesn’t mean customizing a lesson for every student (which many people call personalizing learning), it means making the lesson about the kids in the classroom by engaging them together in the subject at hand. This resonates nicely with the KQED post on how teen brains work, and how helpful it is to knowing what’s important to kids.

Also this week, find several meaningful stories on civil rights in the Diversity/Inclusion section. These have particular resonance on MLK day. For a (very) small collection of resources on activities, lessons, and multimedia specific to MLK Day, check out the [Martin Luther King Jr Day (MLK Day)](https://app.athenalab.io/topics/1309?view=items) topic on Athena Lab, which references materials from Facing History and Ourselves, PBS Newshour, and more.

Also, can it really be that the excellent film “Most Likely to Succeed” came out ten years ago? Apparently so! Find an excellent post in the Pedagogy section reminding us of how powerful the film is.

Last, see the AI update for many excellent resources, especially pairs of posts on the extraordinary explosion of AI companions as well as the growing signal that AI tutors seem to be contributing meaningfully to student progress in several new reports.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
2025-01-19.ai_intro_md:
#### AI companions, virtual tutors, and student perceptions of acceptable use of AI

I have suggested in the past that AI companions are going to have the most significant impact on us of all the changes AI brings. I didn’t think it would happen as fast as it is happening. See both of the feature articles this week for how AI companions are both settling down and upending the lives of individuals from very different places in life. One story tracks people in their 60s whose AI companions bring intellectual conversation, romance, healing, and more. And in the other, hear about a 28 year woman whose AI companion serves as something like a surrogate husband while she and her husband are temporary in different places. Both articles reference risk and concern about AI companions and adolescents.

Also this week, find several posts on about productive applications of AI tutors. More and more narratives are recognizing that AI will not replace teachers, but it will support learning. Exactly how this comes together will be the work of the years ahead. But it’s beginning to take shape.

Also this week, see the Pew Research report on US teens’ use of ChatGPT for homework. Very helpful information on student usage, demographics, perceptions, and more.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2025-01-26.intro_md:
#### Creativity in education, think-pair-share variations, evolutions of DEI, Excel World Championships, and more

What a joy it was this past week to join Nat Damon for a conversation about creativity and education on his podcast “Reach. Teach. Talk.”  Nat is the author of [Time to Teach: Time to Reach](https://www.amazon.com/Time-Teach-Teachers-Relational-Teaching/dp/1999663705), and his work explores the centrality of relationships in student development and learning. In our chat, we dove into the creative lives of teachers, creativity in the curriculum, and more. Find our conversation on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zekVgMH3krE), [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/7crs4wqvlUb20fZnoEP0qx?si=opiDt8mvS4i_wAGonrVGmw&nd=1&dlsi=431541f394944d80), and [Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-power-of-relational-creativity/id1493453131?i=1000685363949).

In this issue, find a feature on the ever-useful think-pair-share. The post posits that varying the T-P-S activity can keep it fresh for students while still leaning into its pedagogical utility for teachers. Find 16 approaches in the post. Also featured this week is an excellent series of vignettes by research assistant Billy Oppenheimer on people who changed the trajectory of their lives by surrounding themselves with different peers. It’s an excellent and inspiring look at the peer effect, which we think about often in relation to students and how the classmates around them shape so much of who they become.

Also this week, find posts on social media, close reading, collaborative grading and even, for the surprising delight of it, the latest Microsoft Excel World Championship, in which people create interactive games solely from spreadsheets.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
2025-01-26.ai_intro_md:
#### How does AI affect learning?

Now over two years since the arrival of ChatGPT, studies are beginning to gain a critical mass of insight into the effect of AI on student learning. It isn’t earth shattering: so far, AI helps some kinds of learning and jeopardizes others. How effective it is depends on how it is used. This is ever the case with a new technology. The lessons to be learned from these studies are in the details: what is helpful? what isn’t? These are the details we will continue to work out in the years ahead, just as we have with other technologies in schools. Find a number of these recent studies in Dr. Philippa Hardman’s post in features.

Also in the features, find OpenAI’s announcement of their first AI agent. It’s designed to be able to control your computer and take action on your behalf. This is either the true beginning of everyone having an assistant, or it is the beginning of an AI-takeover dystopia. Or both!

Also this week, use cases of AI continue to expand. See the post in education on GenAI use cases for historians — and also, later on, the post about how the CIA is exploring use of AI.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
