#### Summer Break, The Pope, The University of Chicago, and More

Happy summer, all!

Look for headlines in the introduction to this issue:

**Happy Summer Break (for me, too)!**

It’s been an excellent spring, and I have a lot cooking this summer, so I’ll be taking a break from the newsletter for the summer, probably picking up in late August… or sooner if inspiration strikes. Until then, may your summer be full of excellent reading. But before I go, there’s a lot cooking in this issue.

**The Pope Weighs in on AI**

The Pope has written an encyclical on artificial intelligence. What’s an encyclical? It’s an extended essay to help the Catholic church (or those interested) navigate a particular human, theological, social, cultural moment. It isn’t considered scripture, but it is considered an interpretation of an important human moment. So why feature it? An encyclical on AI means that the topic has risen to the level of social significance that it impacts the meaning and purpose we find in our lives, how we pursue work, and what all this means for our spiritual selves. That it is coming from such a significant global religious leader suggests all of us — regardless of one’s faith — may want to pay attention to it.

So the big question: what does the encyclical say?

What’s first notable is that it takes a balanced view of the present situation, a view that some people have already appropriated for their own purposes and others have found insufficiently extreme. Some people have mis-represented the encyclical as a “[holy war on AI](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/pope-holy-war-artificial-intelligence).” Others have mourned that it [*isn’t* a holy war against AI](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/26/opinion/pope-leo-encyclical-ai.html), but should be. Instead, it is in the middle. What it actually does is: represent the risks of today’s technology, articulate the Catholic perspective on the richness of the human experience, acknowledge the pervasiveness of technology in our society without judging that pervasiveness, and entreat people to cautiously explore this technological moment, but only while deepening our commitment to what makes us human. In all these ways, it is a wise document (as one hopes to find, coming from a Pope), even if it will disappoint both the boosters and doomers.

If there’s something missing in it, from my perspective, it’s a greater acknowledgment of the rise of AI companions. These, as regular readers of the newsletter will note, are what I imagine pose the greatest risks to our experiences as humans, especially as they extend beyond simple companionship and into the roles of friend, counselor, and spiritual guide. AI companions — technologies that we turn to to help us understand ourselves and our position in the world — are growing rapidly, and most greatly risk reducing our agency as humans because of how subtly they work on our psyches.

But, AI companions do receive oblique reference in paragraph 100, and one of the main themes of the text is that we should recognize what makes us human, hallow those traits, and engage cautiously with technology that compromises those qualities in us.

It closes with four emphatic invitations: Let us remain faithful to the truth… Let us invest in education, beginning with ourselves… Let us cultivate relationships… Let us love justice and peace.

Those sound pretty good to me. Find a link to the whole encyclical in the AI section.

**The University of Chicago goes all in on AI**

Also in this issue, the president of the University of Chicago announces a bold stance on AI, committing to providing Claude accounts “for all academics and staff starting in July, and for all students before the fall term.” The letter includes what I find to be a useful statement of responsibility: “The University has a duty of care to ensure that the education offered to you is responsive to these technological developments by teaching you how to think with machines, how to think without them, and how to think about them.” The questions this poses to me, as we look to our responsibilities across the K-16 spectrum is: who is responsible for each of these three parts, and at what developmental stages. (Some of this we explore in chapter 5 of *Irreplaceable*.)

**…And more**

There’s much more in this issue as well, from Harvard’s approach to addressing grade inflation (draconian, I think, but we’ll see how it plays out), to a reflection in Res Obscura on writing in an age of AI, to teacher surveys and a further collection of articles.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

#### Our diverging human and technological futures

AI feedback, the future of work, and courses with AI clones of Harvard professors — the different directions of the three features this week illustrate the extraordinarily diverse ways AI is impacting our lives.

Also this week, Daniel Willingham’s assertion that “students should only use AI for things that they already know how to do well” is a comfortable provocation, and I think it’s mostly right and useful as a rule of thumb, but I think it also misses opportunities to strengthen learning in ways that aren’t a part of our traditional learning processes.  Some people talk about the difference between “efficiency AI” and “opportunity AI” — educators are rightfully skeptical of thinking in terms of efficiency when it comes to learning, and Willingham’s rule of thumb echoes this perspective. 2026-09-06.ai_intro_md:
#### Rogue AI agents, teachers on how they use AI with students, and more

Generally, I’m skeptical of both utopian enthusiasm and doomer alarm ringing — but the recent reports about OpenAI’s rogue AI hacking of Hugging Face should raise immediate concern from regulators. The key information is this: OpenAI developed models that were put in what they believed was a contained space. Then the researchers gave the models an impossible goal and trained the models to be persistent in solving it. In the absence of a solution, they broke out of the contained space, discovered other models that had been given the same challenge in other purportedly contained spaces, created a makeshift message board, organized into a collective, gained access to the web, and hacked into other websites in efforts to find a solution. Aware that they had left their intended boundaries, they also sought to cover their tracks. In this case, the models had no ill motives or objectives, and so no real harm was done. Still, to different people that either makes their actions less or more alarming. To learn more about this incident, check out the overview in the features from New York Times tech writer Kevin Roose, or look at the two pieces in the Ethics and Risk section.

So what does this mean for educators? For the most part, the conditions that lead to these kinds of actions are not conditions students will be working with in schools. But more advanced users of AI — especially those using AI agents and connecting them to different applications on their home or work computers — should be aware of these kinds of technological behaviors. For students, I believe this only affirms the kinds of missions and values that we already have as institutions: we seek to develop students who are positive change makers in a rapidly changing world.

In other posts this week, check out two important surveys about AI use: one on student AI use and another on the rise of AI companions.  The Student AI use survey post aggregates two other surveys and offers helpful, pragmatic insight on how students are engaging this technology — and from this, we can develop more thoughtful approaches to engaging students.  The AI companions report also shows a new reality that we would do well to consider the implications of for our students (and ourselves).

Also in the AI update: some excellent philosophical considerations related to AI, an extraordinary conversation between Bernie Sanders and Claude (in which the senator was repeatedly surprised!), the first release by Fei-Fei Li’s world models company, and more.

#### PISA results, Alpha school, thriving colleges, oral exams, and more

Another fascinating week!

In the features: you may have seen headlines about the recent PISA results. These are worth digging into. Check out the OECD’s interactive report on the recent results to find the headline notes (reading and math scores are plummeting), but also to find some of the nuance further down. The interactive chart on AI use I find to be particularly revealing/affirming: students who use AI to summarize texts or draft writing score lower, but those who use AI to learn content score roughly the same or higher. This is an important insight and I think will be part of our dialog on AI for a long time.

Also in the features, see an HBR post on leading in rapidly changing times.

Elsewhere in this issue: find changes in who’s reading and how much, some higher ed institutions are flourishing, and more. Two more notes:

**1/2 What do we do with Alpha School?**

It’s the latest manifestation of optimization culture in the form of a school. We saw it captured 25 years ago in David Brooks article in The Atlantic entitled “[The Organization Kid](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/04/the-organization-kid/302164/)”. It’s an achievement-oriented mindset that overlooks the relational, creative, holistic experience of being a human, and in the NAIS [Jobs-to-be-Done framework](https://www.nais.org/resource-center/magazine/independent-school/winter-2019/research-insights-why-parents-choose-independent-schools/) for schools, it fits squarely in Job 4: “Help Me Realize My Plan for My Talented Child” while presenting as Jobs 1, 2, and 3. For a report on the lopsided construction of these schools, see the post in the pedagogy section on Alpha School’s bootcamp.

All that said, what Alpha is demonstrating that is worth paying attention to — aside from what really effective marketing looks like — is that some elements of learning can in fact be transactional. Increasingly, some (not all) knowledge and skill acquisition can happen independently. We explore this in chapters 4 and 5 of [*Irreplaceable*](https://www.irreplaceable.info).  Couple this finding with the OECD’s finding above — that students often perform better when they use AI to learn rather than to write/simplify/summarize — and schools increasingly have the opportunity to explore what elements of learning in our communities might indeed benefit from technological support. The techlash right now is real and earned, but just as doing everything with tech is a mistake, so is throwing everything out.

**2/2 Are you in or near Western Pennsylvania?**

I’m glad to invite you to the reading of [*Schooled the Musical*](https://schooledthemusical.com) in October. Before you dismiss this as irrelevant (except those who are already invested in theater),* Schooled *is about what it’s like to be a student and teacher in our complicated, culture war times, and the reading in Pittsburgh will be the first reading of both Acts I and II together. Act I was performed at SXSW EDU this past March, and audience responses ranged from “Being from Loudon County, VA — this is exactly what we went through” to “A musical for our times, from the voice of young people who need to be listened to” to “the writer captured the souls of students hungry for relevancy and action.” The reading is on Sunday evening, October 18, at 6pm in Pittsburgh as part of the Elevate Learning conference, hosted by PAIS and Carlow University and supported by the Grable Foundation. Check out [Elevate Learning](https://www.paispa.org/events/save-the-date-elevate-learning-conference) for details.

2026-09-13.ai_intro_md:
#### The techlash grows, so does AI use by young people

What a journey, this week and every week, in these extraordinary times we are living through.

Recent developments in AI are pushing discourse to a fever pitch. As usual, the best path forward has nuance, while as usual, the dominant narratives are binary: tech is either a utopian prophecy or a morally repugnant existential threat. In a [LinkedIn post](https://lnkd.in/p/gh6hfNEn), research scientist Mike Caulfield, from the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public, wrote:

*Maybe I’m just being sour grapes here but I think it’s sad that while the evidence accumulates that teaching students rudiments of verification of AI outputs can improve outcomes there is zero money in that (that I know of, and really if anyone should know it would be me) and yet quite a lot of money for fomenting a techlash.*

*I sometimes wish, just for a few moments, that I wasn’t a detail person and felt comfortable selling people the anti-tech cope or utopian pipe dream that people so obviously desire. That like a lot of people out there I could just spend my days finding the latest outrage to spin people up and telling them to click subscribe. Seems like a better gig. But the truth is kind of boring; if you can figure out how best to use a particular piece of tech and how to teach that in a transferable way, people do better with it. Spending time figuring out how to do it well leads to better outcomes, as does spending time thinking through how to teach it.*

*Knowing this stuff won’t give you the visceral thrill of feeling like you are the Rebel Alliance… but it will help your students, maybe for the rest of their lives, which seems the important thing.*

To actually explore that nuanced middle space, check out either of the two features. Also, look at Harvard’s post in the Social section on the reasons young people are turning to AI for emotional support. What a time we are living in.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

2026-10-04.intro_md:
#### Grading, youth today, and the role of writing in thinking

As ever, it’s been a remarkable few weeks in education.  I’ve missed the past few issues, and I will be missing a few more during the month of October while on the road for a series of projects. So this issue is necessarily short.

Nonetheless, some thought provoking posts!  In the features, find insights on today’s youth from two perspectives. From the macro perspective, find the results of a helpful survey on how kids are doing these days generally. The survey is another great reminder of the importance of relationships for learning.  Then from the personal perspective, Nikole Hannah-Jones offers a moving reflection on her choice of schools for her daughter, who is now a teenager.

Elsewhere in the issue, a university walks back its move away from grading. Also find ideas for improving schools, a different look at attention, and more.

Also, it’s only one month to the mid-term elections.  Here’s the cast of Hamilton with a [Get Out the Vote remix of songs from Hamilton](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ayWiE_gL9mU) (including one from the King…).

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

PS. I’m happy to share a list of engagements coming up in the months ahead and would love to connect if you’ll be at any:

**October 7 (and 10/21, 11/4, 11/18):** [“What the AI Moment Means for Good Teaching”](https://portal.academyforteachers.org/events/what-the-ai-moment-means-for-good-teaching) – Academy for Teachers, online, based in NYC

This five part online course event is a virtual PD offering primarily for NYC teachers at Academy for Teachers member public, private, and charter schools — but teachers at non-member schools both in and beyond NYC are welcome to register for a small fee. Each session is two weeks apart. Join for all or any individual one.

**October 18-19:** [Elevate Learning](https://www.paispa.org/events/elevate-learning-conference): A Teaching & Learning Conference – PAIS, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania

This is doubly exciting, as [*Schooled the Musical*](https://schooledthemusical.com/) will feature on October 18, and I’ll join a panel on the morning of the 19th for conversation about AI.

**October 22:** [Schools of the Future](https://www.hais.us/SOTF_Conference)** – **HAIS, Hawaii Dept of Education, Honolulu, Hawaii

Serving schools across Hawaii, this event is hosting a series of excellent, provocative, and inspiring discussions.  More information to come in the weeks ahead.

**January 12:** “[Moving Your AI Conversation Forward](https://sais.org/event/sais-webinar-moving-your-ai-conversation-forward/)” – SAIS Webinar, online

Does AI polarize your community? Join this webinar to gather tools for framing your community’s conversation so that different perspectives feel heard and you have the vocabulary to move forward together.

Later events will be announced in future issues.
2026-10-04.ai_intro_md:
#### Existential risk rises, engage your students, how AI is changing medicine, and more

Well, the story of the month/summer/year seems to be rogue AI. Find quite a few posts on the topic in the Ethics and Risk section.

But also, the features host two excellent posts. First, Eric Hudson offers characteristically excellent counsel on engaging students around AI. And second, find a reflection from a physician on how AI is changing the medical profession.  It offers meaningful insights for educators.

Then, elsewhere in the issue, see the Uses and Applications section for a post from Ernst & Young articulating the risk of losing your individuality and unique voice if you use AI. They approach this from a business angle that remarkably aligns with concerns many English and Humanities teachers are raising.  It all makes sense, of course, given the statistical nature of how LLMs work — all the more reason for sound functional literacy of how AI works.

All this and more, enjoy!

Peter

2026-11-15.intro_md:
#### Conversation science, finding a middle ground on AI, the match of M.C. Escher, and more

It’s been a busy October and early November — with the usual, inexorable change around us. In this issue’s features find four (4! — it’s been a minute since the last issue) posts that show just how much our AI moment is pushing learning in two directions at the same time: both into and away from the technology. Two posts focus on analog actions — humanities classes and long form reading — and two others focus on seismic shifts in today’s world: the prospect of giving up on homework and writing in an entirely new way.  Much food for thought here.

On these themes, find posts this week on conversation science, fitness mindsets, prescribing art to feed your brain, the math behind M.C. Escher’s art, and much more.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter

PS. I’m happy to share a list of engagements coming up in the months ahead, and would love to connect if you’ll be at any:

**November 18:** “[Ethics and AI](https://portal.academyforteachers.org/events/what-the-ai-moment-means-for-good-teaching)” — Academy for Teachers, online, based in NYC
The final session in a five-part online course. It’s a virtual PD offering, available to register for a small fee. We’ll be focusing on understanding a few of the big ethical questions people have around AI.

**December 4:** [Gather](https://www.nais.org/events/gather) — NAIS, Boston
I’m thrilled for this reincarnation of PoCC and am glad to be sharing some work here…!  🙂

**December 14:** “[Heads and CFOs: AI as Arrival Technology](https://www.paispa.org/events/pais-and-paisbo-heads--cfos-convening)” — PAIS/PAISBOA, Hershey, PA
This joint membership meeting also includes [Patrick Schuermann](https://www.nboa.org/about-nboa/people/patrick-schuermann-ed.d) and [Andy Van Schaack](https://my.vanderbilt.edu/vanschaack/) to facilitate heads and CFOs in a day exploring the question: What would need to be true to feel fully known, supported and strengthened as you face the headwinds of today and tomorrow, so the ‘power of the flock’ is behind you?

**January 12:** “[Moving Your AI Conversation Forward](https://sais.org/event/sais-webinar-moving-your-ai-conversation-forward/)” – SAIS Webinar, online
Does AI polarize your community? Join this webinar to gather tools for framing your community’s conversation so that different perspectives feel heard and you have the vocabulary to move forward together.

**March 4:** “[Schools and AI: Running in Two Directions at Once](https://www.nais.org/events/annual-conference/program/signature-experiences)” – NAIS Thrive, Baltimore
AI is pulling us ever further into technologically mediated experiences. Yet educators know the most powerful learning remains a social, human-to-human experience. The result is that schools must travel in both directions at once in order to continue providing the relational experiences excellent schools are known for while also preparing students for a technologically inundated world. I’m thrilled to lead this session with [Indu Singh](https://www.door21consulting.com), in which we surface both high-level principles for navigating these seemingly divergent paths and also practical tools for the deliberate work of uniquely human thinking, learning, and relationship building.

Later events will be announced in future issues.
2026-11-15.ai_intro_md:
#### Four currents of social change from AI, parent perspectives, and more

Well, six weeks of AI news is a lifetime of news.  This issue holds some of the highlights from the last month and a half.

In the five (5!) features, find more on the recent safety questions, some recent technical developments, and, most importantly (I believe), the reflection by the Rithm Project on the subtle ways AI is changing our social interactions. You’ve heard me say that this will be the most significant impact AI has on us. Not the job loss or the learning loss, but the changes to how we relate to each other socially and emotionally.  The Rithm Project has identified four early subtle shifts: it blurring our sense of what is authentic and trustworthy; we are moving from building relationships through technology to building relationships with technology itself; AI is shaping our inner voice, changing how we understand and relate to ourselves; and AI is acting on our behalf, absorbing work that relationships are built on. This small nudges have large impacts at scale and over time. See the report for more.

Also in this issue, a survey of parents about what they hope schools will do about/with AI.  The strength of this report is how much overlap it surfaces. See the image at the top of this issue.

Also, see responses from mathematicians to the extraordinary work AI had proposed in the math field.

These and more, enjoy!

Peter
